Governors in India are selected by the incumbent central government rather than elected, creating a political link to the centre that can constrain state leaders' actions [d3499738s9p0].
The Supreme Court has ruled that governors should be given security of term, but this protection is generally not adhered to in practice [d3499738s9p0].
There are historical examples where governors have acted against state governments, including the 1984 dismissal of the N. T. Rama Rao government and the short-lived appointment of N. Bhaskara Rao as chief minister, illustrating how gubernatorial powers can alter state leadership and policies [d3499738s9p0].
The CBI's attempts to question governors in high-profile matters have encountered claims of immunity and administrative stonewalling by the Union Law Ministry, showing another institutional constraint on investigative agencies seeking testimony from certain officeholders [d3499738s9p0].
